claim: Dog vaccination together with free PEP prevents 71 deaths overall (95% PI: 46-97) at a cost of $1,657 per death averted (95% PI: $1,228-2,526).
source: and preventing 71 deaths overall (95% PIs: 46–97) at a cost of $1,657 per death averted (95% PIs: $1,228–2,526)
evidence: Based on decision tree modeling

claim: Routine dog vaccination would prevent over 300 rabies exposures over ten years (95% PI: 263-401) on Pemba.
source: Since dog vaccination interrupts transmission, we project that routine dog vaccination would mitigate ongoing risks from introductions and keep Pemba rabies-free, and thus prevent over 300 rabies exposures over the ten years (95% PIs: 263–401)
evidence: Based on decision tree modeling projections

claim: Routine dog vaccination would spare around 30 families each year from rabid dog bites and the anxiety of needing to urgently obtain life-saving PEP.
source: sparing around 30 families each year from rabid dog bites and the anxiety of needing to urgently obtain life-saving PEP
evidence: Based on decision tree modeling projections

claim: The cost-effectiveness results remained robust with and without discounting costs.
source: These results remained robust with and without discounting costs (results not shown).
evidence: Based on sensitivity analysis of the model

claim: Metapopulation dynamics maintain dog-mediated rabies via endemically co-circulating viral lineages.
source: Accumulating evidence illustrates how metapopulation dynamics maintain dog-mediated rabies via endemically co-circulating viral lineages (Mancy et al., 2022; Bourhy et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mancy et al., 2022 and Bourhy et al., 2016

claim: Genomic data revealed considerable RABV diversity on Pemba, likely arising from historical introductions.
source: Despite Pemba being a relatively isolated island with a small dog population, genomic data revealed considerable RABV diversity, likely arising from historical introductions, (Brunker et al., 2015)
evidence: Based on genomic analysis with citation to Brunker et al., 2015

claim: The rapid outbreak spread from two contemporary introductions in 2016 highlights the fragility of elimination.
source: The rapid outbreak spread from two contemporary introductions in 2016 highlight the fragility of elimination.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic and epidemiological analysis

claim: While dog rabies remains uncontrolled in nearby populations, reintroduction risks are high.
source: While dog rabies remains uncontrolled in nearby populations, reintroduction risks are high (Bourhy et al., 2016; Zinsstag et al., 2017; Townsend et al., 2013b; Tohma et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Re-emergence is most likely if dog vaccination coverage is low.
source: Re-emergence is most likely if dog vaccination coverage is low, causing major public health and economic consequences (Zinsstag et al., 2017; Tohma et al., 2016; Windiyaningsih et al., 2004; Castillo-Neyra et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Examples from Latin America show dramatic contractions of dog-mediated rabies when dog vaccination is scaled up and sustained.
source: While our study from this small island dog population represents a best-case scenario, examples from Latin America show dramatic contractions of dog-mediated rabies when dog vaccination is scaled up and sustained.
evidence: Based on knowledge of rabies control in Latin America

claim: The last dog-mediated rabies foci in Latin America remain only in very poor communities where dog vaccination has been inadequate.
source: The last dog-mediated rabies foci on the continent remain only in very poor communities where dog vaccination has been inadequate (Vigilato et al., 2013; Rysava et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Vigilato et al., 2013 and Rysava et al., 2020

claim: Routine rabies surveillance in both humans and animals is very weak throughout much of Africa.
source: Our detailed contact tracing data from Pemba contrasts with very weak routine rabies surveillance in both humans and animals throughout much of Africa (Nel, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Nel, 2013

claim: Low case detection leads to underestimation of disease burden, lack of prioritisation, and difficulty ascertaining impacts of control.
source: Low case detection leads to underestimation of disease burden, lack of prioritisation, and difficulty ascertaining impacts of control, including whether disease has been eliminated, or is circulating undetected.
evidence: Based on logical inference about consequences of poor surveillance

claim: The high case detection on Pemba generated confidence that elimination was achieved twice.
source: The high case detection on Pemba generated confidence that elimination was achieved, twice (Townsend et al., 2013a)
evidence: Based on case detection analysis with citation to Townsend et al., 2013a

claim: Much more intensive contact tracing approaches are used in high-income countries in response to rabies incursions.
source: Although contact tracing was intensive compared to routine rabies surveillance which is passive and ad hoc in most African countries, much more intensive approaches are used in high-income countries in response to rabies incursions (Collective french multidisciplinary investigation team, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Collective french multidisciplinary investigation team, 2008

claim: Dog-mediated rabies is considered a public health emergency in high-income countries.
source: highlighting how dog-mediated rabies is considered a public health emergency
evidence: Based on inference from how high-income countries respond to rabies

claim: Only one person (KL) completed all contact tracing on Pemba, while also covering other mainland sites.
source: Only one person (KL) completed all contact tracing on Pemba, while also covering other mainland sites (Lushasi et al., 2021)
evidence: Description of study implementation with citation to Lushasi et al., 2021

claim: Contact tracing was tractable on Pemba given the relatively low incidence of bite patients.
source: Contact tracing was tractable on Pemba given the relatively low incidence of bite patients (in contrast to some Asian settings, Hampson et al., 2019)
evidence: Based on comparison with other settings, with citation to Hampson et al., 2019

claim: A high proportion of bite patients on Pemba were rabies exposures identifiable upon presentation to health facilities.
source: of which a high proportion were rabies exposures identifiable upon presentation to health facilities
evidence: Based on surveillance data

claim: Contact tracing is a vital tool for investigating emerging infectious diseases, such as Ebola.
source: As well as strengthening One Health capacity and intersectoral relationships, contact tracing is a vital tool for investigating emerging infectious diseases, such as Ebola (Faye et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Faye et al., 2015

claim: Contact tracing could be a useful component of rabies control programmes when approaching elimination as caseloads become manageable.
source: Contact tracing could be a useful component of rabies control programmes when approaching elimination as caseloads become manageable.
evidence: Authors' recommendation based on study experience

claim: Without enhanced surveillance during the endgame, incursions would be more likely to go undetected until human deaths occur.
source: Without enhanced surveillance during the endgame, incursions would be more likely to go undetected until human deaths occur (Townsend et al., 2013b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Townsend et al., 2013b

claim: Genomic approaches are increasingly affordable, and capacity for genomic surveillance is growing, accelerated over the course of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.
source: Genomic approaches are also increasingly affordable, and capacity for genomic surveillance is growing, accelerated over the course of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.
evidence: Based on knowledge of genomic surveillance trends

claim: For rabies, genomic approaches have potential to enhance the information that can be gleaned from routine surveillance and inform elimination programmes.
source: For rabies, genomic approaches have potential to enhance the information that can be gleaned from routine surveillance and inform elimination programmes, which are likely to experience such introductions as they progress.
evidence: Authors' assessment based on study findings

claim: There were limitations in reconstructions of transmission events despite high case detection.
source: There were limitations in our reconstructions of transmission events despite high case detection.
evidence: Authors' acknowledgment of study limitations

claim: The study was unable to identify exactly who infected whom within transmission chains, given the low mutation rate of rabies virus and the short intervals between cases.
source: As evident from the tree summaries (Figure 4—figure supplements 2–6), we were unable to identify exactly who infected whom within transmission chains, given the low mutation rate of rabies virus and the short intervals between cases.
evidence: Based on analysis limitations shown in supplementary figures

claim: The study has confidence in the general transmission tree topology and in plausible progenitors within transmission chains.
source: However, we have confidence in the general transmission tree topology and in plausible progenitors within transmission chains (most cases had only a few candidates)
evidence: Based on analysis of transmission tree uncertainty

claim: Estimates of Re and outbreak sizes were robust even with uncertainties in transmission pathways and under alternative pruning algorithms.
source: Moreover, relevant epidemiological inference, such as estimates of Re and of outbreak sizes were robust even with uncertainties in transmission pathways and under alternative pruning algorithms.
evidence: Based on sensitivity analysis of transmission tree methods

claim: The study retrospectively identified a high proportion of cases from their case histories but was less successful in recovering samples (~10% of identified cases overall, increasing to >12% during the outbreak).
source: We caveat that while we retrospectively identified a high proportion of cases from their cases histories, we were less successful in recovering samples (~10% of identified cases overall, increasing to >12% during the outbreak)
evidence: Description of study limitations

claim: The genomic data provided key insights that would not have been evident with only epidemiological data.
source: Nonetheless, the genomic data provided key insights that would not have been evident with only epidemiological data
evidence: Authors' assessment of the value of genomic data

claim: Genomic data showed that rabies was not circulating undetected from 2014-2016 and only re-emerged because of external introductions.
source: first that rabies was not circulating undetected from 2014–2016 (rabies only re-emerged because of external introductions)
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: Genomic data showed that two introductions occurred in 2016 rather than the outbreak arising from a single introduction.
source: second that two introductions occurred in 2016 rather than the outbreak arising from a single introduction (highlighting the non-negligible risk from circulation elsewhere)
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: Genomic data showed it is highly unlikely that other introductions after 2016 established onward transmission.
source: and finally that it is highly unlikely that other introductions after 2016 established onward transmission (whereas the diversity of lineages circulating pre-2014 indicated multiple introductions previously, Brunker et al., 2015)
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis with citation to Brunker et al., 2015

claim: The relatively low mutation rate of rabies may ultimately limit fine-scale inference on who infected whom.
source: Improved sample recovery and sequencing will be valuable for refining methods, but the relatively low mutation rate of rabies may ultimately limit fine-scale inference, on for example, who infected whom.
evidence: Authors' assessment of methodological limitations

claim: The cost per death averted estimate from Pemba is amongst the highest cost-effectiveness estimates of PEP from across Gavi-eligible countries.
source: Our estimate from Pemba is amongst the highest cost-effectiveness estimates of PEP from across Gavi-eligible countries (Hampson et al., 2019)
evidence: Based on comparison with estimates from Hampson et al., 2019

claim: The cost per DALY averted for PEP on Pemba translates to just $13.
source: (translating to a cost of just $13 per DALY averted)
evidence: Based on conversion from cost per death averted

claim: The high cost-effectiveness of PEP on Pemba results from the high proportion of bite patients presenting with rabies exposures rather than bites from healthy dogs.
source: and results from the high proportion of bite patients presenting with rabies exposures rather than bites from healthy dogs
evidence: Based on analysis of surveillance data

claim: In settings with more patients seeking care for healthy dog bites, PEP cost-effectiveness declines.
source: In settings with more patients seeking care for healthy dog bites, PEP cost-effectiveness declines
evidence: Based on inference from cost-effectiveness modeling

claim: Increased vial sharing opportunities under intradermal dose-sparing regimens can slightly offset declines in PEP cost-effectiveness.
source: although this can be slightly offset by increased vial sharing opportunities under intradermal dose-sparing regimens
evidence: Based on inference from cost-effectiveness modeling

claim: PEP does not address the suffering caused from injuries inflicted by rabid animals.
source: Even though PEP is an essential emergency medicine, PEP does not address the suffering caused from injuries inflicted by rabid animals
evidence: Based on logical inference about limitations of PEP

claim: PEP is insufficient to protect the entire at-risk population.
source: and is insufficient to protect the entire at-risk population
evidence: Based on logical inference about limitations of PEP

claim: Lack of awareness, expense and supply issues prevent access to emergency vaccines for marginalised populations.
source: Our study shows how, in practice, lack of awareness, expense and supply issues still prevent access to these emergency vaccines for marginalised populations.
evidence: Based on study findings from contact tracing and case investigations

claim: Mass dog vaccination reduces the risk of exposure and by interrupting transmission in the reservoir can achieve the equitable goal of elimination.
source: In contrast to PEP sustained mass dog vaccination reduces the risk of exposure and by interrupting transmission in the reservoir can achieve the equitable goal of elimination.
evidence: Based on study findings and logical inference

claim: Mass dog vaccination inevitably comes at a higher cost per death averted than PEP.
source: Mass dog vaccination inevitably comes at a higher cost per death averted (Figure 6)
evidence: Based on cost-effectiveness modeling shown in Figure 6

claim: The One Health approach to rabies remains extremely cost-effective compared to other health interventions.
source: Nonetheless compared to other health interventions (Bertram et al., 2021), this One Health approach remains extremely cost-effective.
evidence: Based on comparison with cost-effectiveness benchmarks from Bertram et al., 2021

claim: In denser, more connected populations than Pemba, rabies elimination is likely to take longer and be more fragile.
source: In denser, more connected populations than Pemba rabies elimination is likely to take longer and be more fragile
evidence: Based on inference from study findings

claim: The cost per dog vaccinated is likely to reduce in areas with larger dog populations and with opportunities for optimising the delivery of dog vaccination.
source: while conversely the cost per dog vaccinated is likely to reduce in areas with larger dog populations and with opportunities for optimising the delivery of dog vaccination
evidence: Based on inference about economies of scale

claim: The cost-effectiveness estimates from Pemba lie within expectations for countries in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Our cost-effectiveness estimates lie within expectations for countries in sub-Saharan Africa (Hampson et al., 2019)
evidence: Based on comparison with estimates from Hampson et al., 2019

claim: The transferability of cost-effectiveness estimates from Pemba is limited by various considerations.
source: but these considerations limit their transferability
evidence: Authors' acknowledgment of limitations in generalizability

claim: The relationship between dog vaccination coverage and risk reduction needs to be better quantified to improve health economic models.
source: To improve health economic models, the relationship between dog vaccination coverage and risk reduction needs to be better quantified
evidence: Authors' recommendation for future research

claim: Research is needed on health seeking behaviours following bites by both healthy and rabid dogs that impact cost-effectiveness.
source: and research is needed on health seeking behaviours following bites by both healthy and rabid dogs that impact cost-effectiveness
evidence: Authors' recommendation for future research

claim: Realised cost-effectiveness depends on the stochastic nature of outbreaks and the degree to which interventions are delivered as intended.
source: Moreover, realised cost-effectiveness depends on the stochastic nature of outbreaks and the degree to which interventions are delivered as intended, including how dog vaccination coverage is maintained, since vaccination campaigns can often lapse, as seen from Pemba.
evidence: Based on study findings and logical inference

claim: The COVID-19 pandemic highlights how disruption can severely set back rabies programmes.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic highlights how such disruption can severely set back rabies programmes (Kunkel et al., 2021; Raynor et al., 2021, Nadal et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kunkel et al., 2021; Raynor et al., 2021; and Nadal et al., 2022

claim: The investment needed for a One Health approach to rabies is very cost-effective and can bring rapid success.
source: We conclude that the investment needed for a One Health approach, to support access to life-saving emergency vaccines for bite victims and to achieve and maintain rabies freedom in source populations through dog vaccination is very cost-effective and can bring rapid success.
evidence: Authors' conclusion based on study findings

claim: Lessons from Pemba should build confidence in the feasibility of eliminating rabies elsewhere on the African continent.
source: Lessons from Pemba should build confidence in the feasibility of eliminating rabies elsewhere on the African continent
evidence: Authors' conclusion based on study findings

claim: Lessons from Pemba highlight the importance of sustaining commitment to rabies elimination.
source: but highlight the importance of sustaining commitment
evidence: Authors' conclusion based on study findings

claim: Coordinated dog vaccination over sufficiently large scales will have the greatest and most long-lasting impacts in equitably tackling rabies.
source: Coordinated dog vaccination over sufficiently large scales will have the greatest and most long-lasting impacts in equitably tackling this preventable disease.
evidence: Authors' conclusion based on study findings and inference
